issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a 19-year-old male with stalking trauma, body-focused shame is hard to reconcile unless there was physical or sexual assault. With the given trauma type, this item is clinically incongruent and stands out from the other appraisal items, which are otherwise plausible for stalking.

issues.item: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless the stalker was also a trusted person. Because trauma type has already been fixed as stalking and no other node supplies context supporting an intimate or trusted-perpetrator stalking scenario, this item is clinically questionable in this profile.

issues.item: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' can fit only if the stalker was a trusted person, but the profile gives no other items in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies to support an interpersonal-betrayal formulation. Paired with global characterological self-blame, this creates a specific relational-trauma narrative that is not otherwise represented in the self-report.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is not impossible, but it implies the stalker was a trusted close other. The rest of the profile provides no supporting items in Memory, Threat, Triggers, or Strategies, and with no active formulation edges this appraisal stands as an unsupported trauma-specific claim. The other appraisal items ('I have to be on guard all the time', 'The world is a dangerous place') fit stalking more generically, but the betrayal item makes the node less coherent as a standalone set.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: These two items are not negative appraisals in the usual cognitive sense; they describe ongoing threat monitoring/safety behavior rather than evaluative beliefs. With a formulation showing no active edges and only the Negative Appraisals node populated, selecting predominantly hypervigilance/vigilance items makes the node content misaligned with the intended construct.

vignette: Kwame, a 19-year-old UX designer at a mid-size tech firm in the city, had always imagined his career as a series of creative problem-solving moments. He'd spent nights sketching interface flows and learning the nuances of user testing. But two months ago, a quiet, persistent shadow slipped into that world. It began on a Wednesday afternoon when a man, about the same age as Kwame, started following him down the hallway from his office to the cafeteria. He lingered a few feet behind, his eyes locked on Kwame's backpack as he entered the lunchroom. When Kwame turned to ask if something was wrong, the stranger said nothing, merely smiled and stayed in the background. The next day the same man lingered in the break room while Kwame was preparing a presentation. Each encounter felt more intrusive than the last. He began to feel a knot tightening in his chest when the hallway lights flickered or when he heard the soft thud of someone's shoes echoing down the corridor. Kwame's thoughts settled into a pattern that made the city feel like a place of constant threat. He found himself rehearsing the next steps in his mind before even stepping out of his apartment: "If I step on the curb, I'll see if anyone is behind me." He would pause at each intersection, listening for an unfamiliar tread. The city's usual hum-traffic, people, the hum of office machines-turned into a soundtrack of potential danger. "The world is a dangerous place," he told himself, voice low and urgent. The sense of danger was so vivid that he avoided taking the subway altogether, preferring to walk even on crowded sidewalks, his eyes darting around for any sign of a following figure. At his desk, his fingers hovered over the keyboard as if each keystroke might be overheard. When a client call slipped past the office's open layout, he would feel a surge of anxiety and immediately end the call, fearing a potential eavesdropper. Alongside the constant vigilance, Kwame's internal dialogue grew darker. He began to hold himself responsible for the stalking. "I must have done something to deserve this," he whispered to himself when alone. He blamed his casual attire, his lack of a dark jacket on the cold mornings, even the time he'd forgotten to lock his phone. The self-blame was not an accusation toward anyone else; it was an attempt to make sense of a situation that had no clear origin. He stopped going out for dinner with friends because he feared strangers might be watching, and he kept his personal photos off social media. The isolation compounded his sense that the world, once a place of shared creativity, had turned hostile. Weeks blurred into a cycle of hyper-vigilance. He started avoiding the café on his usual route to work, choosing a different path even though it took an extra fifteen minutes. The change in routine disrupted his client meetings, which often started later than scheduled, forcing him to explain tardiness to colleagues who began to wonder if he was simply unreliable. His project deadlines slipped, and the UX design firm began to question his reliability. Kwame felt a deepening sense of shame. "I can't even trust the people around me," he admitted to a friend during a rare outing at a quiet bookstore. The friend suggested he seek help, but Kwame's mind was already busy dissecting every potential threat. He feared that asking for help might make him appear weak, a weakness that the stalker could exploit. When he finally booked a counseling appointment, it was after a night of restless sleep, his brain replaying the hallway incident over and over. He was terrified that the stalker would show up in the therapist's office, that someone might be listening. He thought, "If I come to the office, I might as well just stay there." Yet he also clung to a fragile hope: that by sharing his experience, he might regain some control, might stop the feeling that the world was unsafe. In the waiting room, he pressed his hands together, knuckles whitening, as the clock ticked slowly. He was scared that he might lose his job, that his career would be ruined, but he was also determined to find a way to stop feeling like he was constantly on guard. The appointment felt like a small, tentative step toward reclaiming his sense of safety in a world that had suddenly seemed full of shadows.
